---
title: "From spreadsheet logic to a computational model"
description: "How the pipeline follows formulas and verifies the extracted model."
---

An Excel workbook is an executable model. Input cells hold assumptions, formula
cells transform them, and output cells expose results. The extraction pipeline
follows this logic and creates an explicit **computational model** of what the
spreadsheet does.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Targets["Selected output cells"] --> Formulas["Follow formula references"]
    Formulas --> Dependencies["Resolve dependencies across sheets"]
    Dependencies --> Graph["Computational model"]
```

## Following the logic

Extraction starts from configured target cells—the results the model is
expected to produce. excel-grapher walks backward through each formula
reference until it reaches workbook leaves such as inputs and constants.

In the resulting dependency graph:

- each cell is a computation or value;
- each formula reference is a dependency;
- cross-sheet references remain explicit;
- constrained dynamic references such as `OFFSET`, `INDIRECT`, and `INDEX` are
  resolved; and
- calculation order follows the graph rather than worksheet position.

This target-driven boundary matters. The computational model contains the logic
required for the selected outputs, rather than assuming that every populated
cell belongs to the public model.

## Inspecting the model

The extract stage writes a dependency-graph explorer under
`artifacts/dependency-graph/`. It lets a reviewer move from an output to its
upstream formulas, inspect cross-sheet paths, and confirm that the expected
inputs were reached.

Run only this first stage with:

```bash
uv run python -m src.extraction_pipeline --extract-graph
```

The graph is also executable. excel-grapher's `FormulaEvaluator` evaluates the
same dependencies in memory, providing a reference implementation for later
code generation.

## How the model is verified

The pipeline uses two differential comparisons:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    Excel["Live Excel workbook"] -->|"Excel versus graph"| Graph["FormulaEvaluator on computational model"]
    Graph -->|"Graph versus Python"| Python["Generated compute functions"]
```

- **Excel versus graph** asks whether extraction preserved workbook behavior.
- **Graph versus Python** asks whether generated code preserved the extracted
  model's behavior.

Both sides receive the same scenario inputs and their outputs are compared
under a defined numerical tolerance. A mismatch fails validation rather than
being explained away by visual inspection.

For the full methodology, acceptance standard, and examples from production
models, see [Proving the Numbers Match](https://teal-insights.github.io/differential-testing/).

::: {.callout-note}
Differential testing establishes computational fidelity over the scenarios
tested. It does not determine whether the spreadsheet's economic assumptions
are correct; that remains a domain-review question.
:::
